title: It is I, fear not (Mark 6:45–56)
hook: he walks on the sea and sees them toiling in rowing

segments.voice: Yesterday, come apart and rest, and five loaves for five thousand. Your line was rest a little. Did you sit down to eat? Tonight the disciples are back on the lake, without him. Day two hundred nine.

Three in the morning. You're pulling at something that won't move. A deadline. A sick child's fever. A relationship that keeps drifting backward no matter how hard you work at it. Your arms ache and you're not getting anywhere, and you're pretty sure no one sees. That's where the disciples are tonight. Right after the feeding of the five thousand, Jesus sends them across the lake by boat while he stays behind to pray. The wind turns against them. They row for hours and get nowhere. Today: it is I.
screen: `THREE IN THE MORNING.` → `PULLING AND GETTING NOWHERE.` → `NO ONE SEES.`

segments.voice: First, he sees. Jesus is on the mountain, praying, and from there he sees them. In the King James: "And he saw them toiling in rowing; for the wind was contrary unto them." They think they're alone out there. They aren't. Second, he comes. In the fourth watch of the night, somewhere between three and six in the morning, he comes to them walking on the sea. And then Mark adds a strange line: he would have passed by them. Why pass by? Scholars point to the Hebrew Bible, where God passes by Moses on the mountain, and passes by Elijah at the cave. Passing by is how God shows himself. Third, the word. The disciples see him and think it's a ghost. They scream. And straightaway he speaks. In the Douay-Rheims: "Have a good heart, it is I, fear ye not." In Mark's Greek, it is I is ego eimi, which can also be heard as I am. Those are the words God speaks to Moses at the burning bush: I am who am. So the same words mean two things at once: it's me, your friend, don't be afraid; and, I am. Fourth, the boat. He climbs in, and the wind drops. And Mark says they were astonished, because they hadn't understood about the loaves; their hearts were hardened. Mark's disciples still don't get it, and he keeps telling us so. Then they land, and people rush the sick to him on mats, begging just to touch the hem of his cloak, and all who touch it are healed. Only Matthew tells of Peter walking on the water. Mark keeps his eyes on the rowers.
screen: `HE SAW THEM TOILING IN ROWING.` · `HE WOULD HAVE PASSED BY.` · `EGO EIMI: IT IS I, I AM.` · `THE WIND DROPS; THEY STILL DON'T SEE.` · then, large: `HAVE A GOOD HEART, IT IS I, FEAR YE NOT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name where you're rowing hard. Settle, and breathe. Picture a small boat at night, and put yourself at the oars. What are you pulling against right now? A task, a person, an illness, a fear. Name it plainly. Notice how tired your arms are. If you pray, you can hear the words spoken into that boat: have a good heart, it is I, fear not. If you don't, simply let your arms rest for two minutes, and let the wind blow. The bell holds the time.
It is I. What Jesus says on the water to his terrified friends: in Greek, ego eimi, it's me, and I am. Today's word.
Your line: it is I. Today, when you're straining at the oars and sure nobody sees, remember the rowers weren't as alone as they thought. Day two hundred nine.

howItsDone: Catholics hear the walking on the water in the weekday Mass readings of the Christmas season, and many pray 'it is I, fear not' in times of fear; the phrase 'be not afraid' became a watchword of Pope John Paul II.

notes: The outline's hook uses the King James 'toiling in rowing' (Douay has 'labouring in rowing'), so the KJV is quoted for 6:48 and named. Douay-Rheims 6:50 given from memory; confirm.
The fourth watch (Roman reckoning, about 3–6 a.m.): confirm.
Passing-by (parerchomai) as a theophany motif echoing Exodus 33–34 and 1 Kings 19: a common scholarly reading; confirm.
Egō eimi as an echo of Exodus 3:14 (Douay 'I am who am'): common reading; stated as 'can also be heard as'.
howItsDone: Mark 6:45–52 is read on a weekday after Epiphany; 'Be not afraid' as John Paul II's watchword (from his inaugural homily, 1978). Confirm both.
